files.codex/u1-teacher-guide.json:
{
  "body": "OBJECTIVES
- Students ask and answer questions about key details in a short informational text read aloud (RI.K.1, SL.K.2).
- Students describe the weather they observe and add a drawing to give more detail (SL.K.4, SL.K.5).
- Students use weather words (sunny, cloudy, rainy, snowy, windy) when they talk about the sky (L.K.6).
- Students sort a week of weather into kinds, count each kind and tell which kind came the most (K.MD.B.3, K.CC.B.5).

MATERIALS
- A class weather chart with a row for each school day and picture cards for sunny, cloudy, rainy, snowy and windy
- A window or doorway where the whole class can see the sky (or a short walk outside)
- Crayons and paper, or tablets with the class activities open for drawing and recording
- Counters or cubes for counting days on the chart

FIVE-DAY PLAN
Day 1: Read Welcome, Weather Watchers! together. Look out the window and name the weather. Choose a weather helper to put today's card on the chart. Keep this routine every day of the semester.
Day 2: Lesson activity: Sky Detectives. Read the text aloud twice. Students answer by speaking, then draw a sky with puffy clouds. Point out real clouds if you can see them.
Day 3: Go outside or to the window. Students start My Weather Picture: look, draw what they see, and record themselves telling about it with the sentence frames.
Day 4: Our Weather Week. Read the week aloud while you point to each day on a chart. Students count the sunny days with counters, then answer. Ask: was this week like our own chart?
Day 5: Assessment: Weather Words Check. Read each question aloud twice. Students answer by speaking, then draw today's weather. Note who still mixes up cloudy and rainy.

DIFFERENTIATION
- Support: give students the five weather picture cards to point to or hold up instead of saying the word. Count days by touching counters one at a time.
- Support: let students use only the first sentence frame and add one word to it.
- Stretch: ask students to use two weather words together (cloudy and windy) and to tell how the weather today is different from yesterday.
- Stretch: count the class chart at the end of each week and say which weather came the least.
- Multilingual learners: teach the weather words with the picture cards and a gesture for each (shiver for snowy, wiggling fingers for rainy, fanning for windy). Invite students to say the word in their home language too, and add those words to the chart.

FAMILY NOTE (send home at the start of the unit)
Our class is becoming Weather Watchers! Every morning we look at the sky and put the weather on our class chart. At home, look outside together and ask your child: is it sunny, cloudy, rainy, snowy or windy today? How do you know? You can count the sunny days this week together too.",
  "id": "u1-teacher-guide",
  "purpose": "context",
  "title": "Teacher guide: Look Up! What Is the Weather?",
  "visibility": "teacher-only"
}

{

files.codex/u2-teacher-guide.json:
{
  "body": "OBJECTIVES
- Students answer questions about key details in a short story read aloud (RL.K.1, SL.K.2).
- Students describe the clothes they would wear in a kind of weather and add a drawing for detail (SL.K.4, SL.K.5).
- Students sort clothes into hot day and cold day groups (L.K.5) and count each group (K.MD.B.3).
- Science focus: people choose clothes to stay warm, dry or cool because the weather changes.

MATERIALS
- A dress-up bag: mittens, a scarf, a coat, rain boots, an umbrella, a sun hat, sunglasses, sandals (or picture cards of each)
- Two hoops or two large paper circles labeled with a sun and a snowflake for sorting
- Crayons and paper, or tablets with the class activities open
- The class weather chart from Unit 1, still updated every morning

FIVE-DAY PLAN
Day 1: Read What Do We Wear? together. Open the dress-up bag one item at a time. Students act out the weather each item is for. Check today's weather on the chart: what should we wear outside today?
Day 2: Lesson activity: What Will Kai Wear? Read the story aloud twice. Students answer by speaking. Ask: what would Kai wear on a rainy day?
Day 3: Dress for a Rainy Day. Read the prompt aloud. Students draw themselves ready for rain and record themselves telling about it. Share a few drawings: what helps us stay dry?
Day 4: Sort the dress-up bag into the sun hoop and the snow hoop as a class, then count each group. Students complete Hot Day or Cold Day? Talk about things that could go in both (a hat).
Day 5: Assessment: Dressed for the Weather Check. Read each question aloud twice. Students speak, draw, and tell why they chose their clothes.

DIFFERENTIATION
- Support: let students point to real items or picture cards before they say or draw them. Accept one clothing word for the snowy question.
- Support: during the sort, give a student only four items and two hoops.
- Stretch: ask what to wear on a day that is both cold and rainy, or on a windy day, and why. Ask students to sort a third group: things for rainy days.
- Multilingual learners: label each item in the dress-up bag with a picture and its English name. Pair students with a partner who shares their home language for the sort, then have them name each item in English.
- Be sensitive about clothing at home: frame questions as "what would you wear" and accept any sensible choice. Keep spare mittens and boots in class if you can.

FAMILY NOTE (send home at the start of the unit)
This week we are learning to dress for the weather. Before you go outside, ask your child to check the sky and choose: do we need a coat, boots, a hat or water today? Ask them to tell you why. Choosing for themselves helps children connect what they see in the sky with how to take care of themselves.",
  "id": "u2-teacher-guide",
  "purpose": "context",
  "title": "Teacher guide: Dress for the Weather",
  "visibility": "teacher-only"
}
files.codex/u3-answer-key.json:
{
  "body": "The Sun Warms Things: 1. It makes the sand warm. 2. A tree blocking the sunlight (anything that blocks the sun). 3. In the shade. 4. Answers vary; a good answer gives a reason, such as \"in the shade, because it is cooler\".\nSun or Shade: Which Is Warmer?: 1. Warm (or hot). 2. Cool (or cooler). 3. The one in the sun. 4. Because the sun shone on it, or because sunlight warms things. 5. Drawing shows one object in the sun and one in the shade. On a cloudy day results may be close; accept \"about the same\" and repeat the test on a sunny day.\nMake Some Shade: the drawing shows something that sits between the sun and the sandbox, such as a roof, an umbrella, a tent, a tree or a sheet on poles, and the student tells that it blocks the sunlight.\nSun and Shade Check: 1. The slide. 2. It is in the shade of the tree; the tree blocks the sunlight. 3. Sunlight (the sun). 4. Cooler. 5. Drawing shows something blocking the sun, such as a tree, umbrella or roof.\nScoring tip: \"the slide is metal\" alone is Getting there on \"I can tell that sunlight warms things\"; look for the sun as the reason. For the design, any idea that blocks sunlight is Got it! even if it would be hard to build.",
  "id": "u3-answer-key",
  "purpose": "answer-key",
  "title": "Answer key: Sun and Shade",
  "visibility": "teacher-only"
}
files.codex/u3-overview.json:
{
  "body": "The sun shines on the ground. ☀️\nSunlight makes the ground warm.\nShade is a place where something blocks the sunlight. 🌳\nShade is cooler.\nIn this unit we will touch, compare and make shade, just like scientists.",
  "id": "u3-overview",
  "purpose": "context",
  "title": "The Warm Sun",
  "visibility": "students"
}
files.codex/u3-teacher-guide.json:
{
  "body": "OBJECTIVES
- Students ask and answer questions about key details in a text read aloud about sunlight (RI.K.1, SL.K.2).
- Students directly compare two objects, one in the sun and one in the shade, to tell which is warmer (K.MD.A.2), and describe what they felt (SL.K.4).
- Students draw and tell about a structure that makes shade, naming what it is and how it helps (W.K.2, SL.K.5).
- Science focus: sunlight warms the Earth's surface; blocking sunlight makes shade, which is cooler.

MATERIALS
- Two matching dark rocks, blocks or squares of dark paper; a sunny spot and a shady spot outside (or a sunny windowsill and a shelf)
- Building materials for shade: craft sticks, paper, cloth scraps, tape, cardboard, clay
- A small tray of sand or soil and a desk lamp, if it is cloudy all week
- Crayons and paper, or tablets with the class activities open

FIVE-DAY PLAN
Day 1: Read The Warm Sun together. In the morning, put one rock in the sun and one in the shade. Ask: what do you think will happen? Leave them until after lunch.
Day 2: Lesson activity: The Sun Warms Things. Read the text aloud twice; students answer by speaking. Then go outside and touch both rocks from Day 1.
Day 3: Sun or Shade: Which Is Warmer? Students repeat the test with two new matching objects, feel them, and record their comparison. Talk about what was the same (the objects) and what was different (sun or shade).
Day 4: Make Some Shade. Read the sandbox problem aloud. Students draw a shade maker and tell how it works. If you can, build a few with craft materials and test them over the sand tray in the sun or under a lamp.
Day 5: Assessment: Sun and Shade Check. Read the story and each question aloud twice. Students answer by speaking and draw one way to make shade.

DIFFERENTIATION
- Support: let students hold both objects at once and say "this one" before naming sun or shade. Offer the words warm, warmer, cool, cooler on picture cards.
- Support: offer a starter drawing of the sandbox so students only add the shade maker.
- Stretch: ask students to test whether a bigger shade maker keeps things cooler than a small one, and to tell which material blocked the most sunlight.
- Multilingual learners: act out warm (fanning) and cool (rubbing arms) and point to the sun and the shade while you say the words. Accept answers in the home language first, then build the English sentence together.
- Safety: on hot days check that metal or dark surfaces are not hot enough to hurt before students touch them, and keep the lamp away from hands.

FAMILY NOTE (send home at the start of the unit)
This week your child is learning that sunlight makes things warm and that shade keeps things cooler. On a sunny day, try this together: touch a sidewalk or step in the sun, then one in the shade. Which is warmer? Ask your child to tell you why. You can also look for shade makers on a walk: trees, umbrellas, porches and awnings.",
  "id": "u3-teacher-guide",
  "purpose": "context",
  "title": "Teacher guide: Sun and Shade",
  "visibility": "teacher-only"
}
files.codex/u4-answer-key.json:
{
  "body": "What Wind Can Do: 1. Air that moves (moving air). 2. You can feel it on your face, and you can see what it moves. 3. Bend tall trees (also push kites and sailboats). 4. Drawing shows something the wind is moving, such as a kite, leaves, a flag or a sailboat.\nWind Hunt: the drawing shows something the wind really moved outside (leaves, grass, a flag, hair, clothes, a streamer), and the student tells what it was and whether the wind was gentle or strong.\nWind Walk Count: 1. 5 leaves. 2. 2 flags. 3. The leaves. 4. The kite (1 kite). 5. 8 things.\nWind Check: 1. Moving air. 2. No, we cannot see it; we know it is there because we feel it and see what it moves. 3. The strong wind. 4. Any thing wind pushes: leaves, a kite, a flag, a sailboat, a pinwheel, clouds. 5. Drawing shows something being moved by the wind (bent trees, flying leaves, a kite).\nScoring tip: on \"I can tell what wind is\", a student who says \"it blows things\" is Getting there; \"air that moves\" is Got it! When counting, a student who counts all 8 correctly but mixes up which group is biggest is Got it! on counting and Getting there on comparing.",
  "id": "u4-answer-key",
  "purpose": "answer-key",
  "title": "Answer key: Wind on the Move",
  "visibility": "teacher-only"
}
files.codex/u4-overview.json:
{
  "body": "Wind is moving air. 🌬️\nWe cannot see the wind.\nBut we can feel it, and we can see what it moves!\nWind makes leaves dance 🍂, flags wave and kites fly 🪁.\nIn this unit we will go on a wind hunt and find out what the wind can push.",
  "id": "u4-overview",
  "purpose": "context",
  "title": "We Cannot See the Wind",
  "visibility": "students"
}
files.codex/u4-teacher-guide.json:
{
  "body": "OBJECTIVES
- Students ask and answer questions about key details in a text read aloud about wind (RI.K.1, SL.K.2).
- Students observe and describe things moved by the wind, adding a drawing for detail (SL.K.4, SL.K.5).
- Students sort what they saw into groups, count each group and say which has the most and the fewest (K.MD.B.3, K.CC.B.5).
- Science focus: wind is moving air; we know it is there because we feel it and see what it pushes, and a stronger wind pushes harder.

MATERIALS
- Paper pinwheels or streamers on sticks (one per student or pair)
- A hand fan or folded paper fans for gentle and strong wind
- Light and heavy objects to test: a feather, a tissue, a crayon, a block
- Clipboards with three tally rows (leaves, flags, other) for the wind walk
- Crayons and paper, or tablets with the class activities open

FIVE-DAY PLAN
Day 1: Read We Cannot See the Wind together. Students wave paper fans at their own faces: can you feel the air move? Can you see it? Check the weather chart: is today windy?
Day 2: Lesson activity: What Wind Can Do. Read the text aloud twice; students answer by speaking and draw something the wind pushes. Test fans on a feather and a block: which one moves?
Day 3: Wind Hunt. Take pinwheels or streamers outside. Students look for things the wind moves, then draw one and record themselves telling about it. If the day is calm, use fans in class and try again on a breezier day.
Day 4: Wind Walk Count. Read the class wind walk aloud while you show 5, 2 and 1 counters. Students count each group and compare. Make your own tally on a real wind walk if the weather allows.
Day 5: Assessment: Wind Check. Read the pinwheel story and each question aloud twice. Students answer by speaking and draw a windy day.

DIFFERENTIATION
- Support: let students blow on a pinwheel gently and then hard before answering which spins faster. Use counters lined up in rows for counting.
- Support: accept "it moves things" as a first answer to "what is wind", then model "wind is moving air" and have students echo it.
- Stretch: ask which objects the gentle wind could move and which only the strong wind could move, and why. Ask how many more leaves than flags we saw.
- Multilingual learners: teach gentle and strong with a small and a big fan motion. Use the frames with pictures (a leaf, a flag, a kite) beside each blank.
- Calm week? Wind changes from day to day. Keep the pinwheels by the window and return to the wind hunt on the first windy day.

FAMILY NOTE (send home at the start of the unit)
This week we are learning about wind. Wind is moving air: we cannot see it, but we can feel it and see what it moves. On a walk or from a window, play "wind detective" with your child: what is the wind moving right now? Is it a gentle wind or a strong wind? You can make a simple streamer from a strip of paper and a stick and watch it together.",
  "id": "u4-teacher-guide",
  "purpose": "context",
  "title": "Teacher guide: Wind on the Move",
  "visibility": "teacher-only"
}
files.codex/u5-answer-key.json:
{
  "body": "Where Does Rain Go?: 1. From the clouds. 2. With their roots. 3. The sun warms it, the water goes up into the air, and the puddle gets smaller until it is gone. 4. Drawing shows rain drops falling on a plant.\nOur Rain Cup: 1. Tuesday (5 is more than 2). 2. Wednesday (3 is less than 5). 3. Tuesday. 4. Drawing shows the cup with water up to line 5.\nWhere Did the Puddle Go?: the first picture shows a big puddle; the second shows a small puddle or a dry spot with the sun. The student tells it in order: the puddle was big, the sun warmed it, the puddle got smaller or dried up.\nRain and Water Check: 1. From the clouds. 2. Plants (also trees, grass, animals, people). 3. Thursday (4 is more than 1). 4. The sun warms it and the water goes into the air. 5. Drawing shows a puddle getting smaller or gone, with the sun.\nScoring tip: kindergartners do not need the word evaporate; \"the sun dried it up\" or \"the water went into the air\" is Got it! A student who says the puddle \"went into the ground\" is partly right (some water does soak in) and is Getting there if they do not mention the sun.",
  "id": "u5-answer-key",
  "purpose": "answer-key",
  "title": "Answer key: Rain and Water",
  "visibility": "teacher-only"
}
files.codex/u5-overview.json:
{
  "body": "Rain falls from gray clouds. 🌧️\nRain makes puddles on the ground.\nPlants drink the rain. 🌱\nWhen the sun comes out, puddles dry up. ☀️\nIn this unit we will catch rain in a cup and find out where puddles go.",
  "id": "u5-overview",
  "purpose": "context",
  "title": "Drip, Drop, Rain!",
  "visibility": "students"
}
files.codex/u5-teacher-guide.json:
{
  "body": "OBJECTIVES
- Students ask and answer questions about key details in a text read aloud about rain (RI.K.1, SL.K.2).
- Students compare rain amounts by comparing numbers from 1 to 10 (K.CC.C.7) and by comparing water heights directly (K.MD.A.2).
- Students draw and tell, in order, how a puddle changes after a sunny day (W.K.3, SL.K.5).
- Science focus: rain falls from clouds; it soaks into the ground, plants take it up, and puddles dry up when the sun warms them.

MATERIALS
- A clear, straight-sided cup or jar with lines drawn and numbered 1 to 10 (a class rain gauge), set outside where it will not tip over
- A spray bottle and a tray of soil with a small plant, for showing rain soaking in
- Chalk, for tracing around a real puddle (or a puddle you make with a cup of water on the playground)
- Crayons and paper, or tablets with the class activities open

FIVE-DAY PLAN
Day 1: Read Drip, Drop, Rain! together. Set up the class rain cup outside. Ask: where do you think rain goes after it lands? Keep checking the cup each morning with the weather chart.
Day 2: Lesson activity: Where Does Rain Go? Read the text aloud twice; students answer by speaking and draw rain on a plant. Spray water on the soil tray and watch it soak in.
Day 3: Make or find a puddle on a sunny morning. Trace around it with chalk. Check it again after lunch and trace it again. Students begin Where Did the Puddle Go? and tell first, then, last.
Day 4: Our Rain Cup. Read the three days aloud while you show the numbers on a drawn cup. Students compare the numbers and draw Tuesday's cup. Compare with your real rain cup if it has rained.
Day 5: Assessment: Rain and Water Check. Read each question aloud twice. Students answer by speaking and draw a drying puddle.

DIFFERENTIATION
- Support: give students a number line from 1 to 10 to touch while comparing: the number further along is more. Show water heights with cubes stacked to each line.
- Support: for the puddle, give two boxes labeled First and Then so students draw one picture in each.
- Stretch: ask how much more rain fell on Tuesday than on Monday (3 lines more), and where the water from the puddle went.
- Multilingual learners: teach puddle, soak, dry up and cloud with gestures and the real puddle. Let students tell the puddle story first in their home language, then in English with the frames.
- Dry weather? If it does not rain this week, fill the rain cup with a watering can to show each day's amount, and say so, so students know it was a model.

FAMILY NOTE (send home at the start of the unit)
This week we are learning where rain comes from and where it goes. After it rains, look for a puddle with your child. Ask: what will happen to the puddle when the sun comes out? Check it again later in the day and see if it got smaller. If you like, put a straight-sided cup outside on a rainy day and look at how much rain it caught.",
  "id": "u5-teacher-guide",
  "purpose": "context",
  "title": "Teacher guide: Rain and Water",
  "visibility": "teacher-only"
}
files.codex/u6-answer-key.json:
{
  "body": "The Four Seasons: 1. The four seasons (how the weather changes over the year). 2. They change color and fall down. 3. Cold; in some places it snows. 4. Rain (and warmer weather). 5. Fall.\nMy Favorite Season: any season is right. The drawing shows weather that fits that season, and the reason uses the weather or what the student does in it (\"I like winter because I can play in the snow.\").\nFall Week, Winter Week: 1. 3 sunny days. 2. 3 snowy days. 3. The fall week (3 is more than 1). 4. It got colder: fewer sunny days and some snowy days.\nSeasons Check: 1. Winter. 2. Fall. 3. Spring. 4. Spring. 5. Drawing shows a sunny, warm day and summer clothes such as shorts, a sun hat or sandals.\nScoring tip: where winters are mild, accept \"rainy\" or \"cool\" as winter weather if it matches your chart. A favorite season with no reason is Getting there on \"I told why, using the weather\".",
  "id": "u6-answer-key",
  "purpose": "answer-key",
  "title": "Answer key: Four Seasons",
  "visibility": "teacher-only"
}
files.codex/u6-overview.json:
{
  "body": "There are four seasons: fall 🍂, winter ❄️, spring 🌷 and summer ☀️.\nEach season has its own kind of weather.\nOur weather chart helps us see the weather change.\nIn this unit we will talk about the seasons and tell which one we like best.",
  "id": "u6-overview",
  "purpose": "context",
  "title": "Weather Changes",
  "visibility": "students"
}
files.codex/u6-teacher-guide.json:
{
  "body": "OBJECTIVES
- Students identify the main topic and retell key details of a text read aloud about the seasons (RI.K.2, RI.K.1, SL.K.2).
- Students state a favorite season and give a reason using the weather, with a drawing (W.K.1, SL.K.5).
- Students count and compare the kinds of weather in two weeks of a weather chart (K.MD.B.3, K.CC.C.6).
- Science focus: weather follows a pattern over the year; each season tends to bring its own kind of weather, and our daily chart lets us see the change.

MATERIALS
- The class weather chart, with the first weeks of school saved; if you have them, photos of the schoolyard in different seasons
- Four large cards: fall, winter, spring, summer, with a picture on each
- Counters in two colors for comparing weeks
- Crayons and paper, or tablets with the class activities open

FIVE-DAY PLAN
Day 1: Read Weather Changes together. Look back at the first week on our weather chart and compare it with this week. Ask: has the weather changed since school started?
Day 2: Lesson activity: The Four Seasons. Read the text aloud twice. Students answer by speaking. Put the four season cards in order in a circle and walk around it: after summer comes fall again.
Day 3: Fall Week, Winter Week. Show each week with counters, one color per kind of weather. Students count and compare, then say how the weather changed. Then count our own chart from September the same way.
Day 4: My Favorite Season. Students draw themselves outside in their favorite season and record why they like it. Graph the class's favorite seasons with sticky notes.
Day 5: Assessment: Seasons Check. Read each question aloud twice. Students answer by speaking and draw a summer day.

DIFFERENTIATION
- Support: use the four season cards for every question so students can point before they speak. Count with counters in a line.
- Support: give students the reason frame with picture choices (snow, leaves, flowers, sun) to finish "I like it because ___."
- Stretch: ask students to give two reasons for their favorite season, or to tell one thing they do in each season.
- Multilingual learners: name each season with its card and a gesture (falling leaves, shivering, a growing flower, wiping a hot brow). Invite families to share how seasons work where they have lived.
- Local climate: not every place has snowy winters or colorful fall leaves. Use your own weather chart as the main evidence, accept answers that match where students live, and say so: "in some places it snows; here, winter is rainy".

FAMILY NOTE (send home at the start of the unit)
This week we are learning about the four seasons and how the weather changes over the year. Ask your child: what is your favorite season, and why? Look through family photos together and guess the season in each one from the weather and the clothes. Talk about what the weather is like here in each season.",
  "id": "u6-teacher-guide",
  "purpose": "context",
  "title": "Teacher guide: Four Seasons",
  "visibility": "teacher-only"
}
files.codex/u7-answer-key.json:
{
  "body": "Storm Smart: 1. Go inside a building right away. 2. Until the storm is over. 3. Studies the sky and tells us what weather is coming. 4. Drawing shows a building (a house or school) with the student inside.\nSafe Inside: the drawing shows the student inside a building (a home, school or store), away from the storm, and the student tells that they go inside and stay there until the storm is over. Under a tree or on the playground is Not yet.\nWeather Reporter: answers depend on the day. A full report names the weather, clothes that fit it, and a matching tip (for example, sunny and hot: wear a hat, drink water; rainy: wear boots; cold: wear mittens; thunder: stay inside).\nWeather Safety Check: 1. {
  "body": "OBJECTIVES
- Students ask and answer questions about key details in a text read aloud about storm safety (RI.K.1, SL.K.2).
- Students draw and tell about a safe place in a thunderstorm, naming what to do (SL.K.5, W.K.2).
- Students give a short weather report, describing the weather, what to wear and a safety tip in a clear voice (SL.K.4, SL.K.6).
- Science focus: weather forecasts help people prepare for severe weather; in a thunderstorm we go inside a building, in heat we drink water and find shade, and in cold we cover up.

MATERIALS
- Your school's severe-weather drill plan (where the class goes and the signal you use)
- A pretend microphone and a weather map drawn on chart paper, for the Weather Reporter
- The weather chart and dress-up bag from earlier units
- Crayons and paper, or tablets with the class activities open

FIVE-DAY PLAN
Day 1: Read Weather Safety together. Teach the rule "when thunder roars, go indoors" with a call and response. Show where our class goes in a storm drill.
Day 2: Lesson activity: Storm Smart. Read the text aloud twice; students answer by speaking and draw a safe place. Talk about how a forecast helps grown-ups plan (bring an umbrella, move recess inside).
Day 3: Safe Inside. Read the prompt aloud with a thunder sound if you have one. Students draw where they would go and record themselves telling what they would do. Review heat and cold safety with the dress-up bag.
Day 4: Weather Reporter. Model a 20-second report: today's weather, what to wear and a safety tip. Students look outside, practice with a partner and record their report. Play a few for the class.
Day 5: Assessment: Weather Safety Check. Read each question aloud twice. Students answer by speaking and draw themselves staying safe. Celebrate the semester: every student is a Weather Watcher!

DIFFERENTIATION
- Support: practice the thunder rule with a gesture (hands cupped to ears, then pointing indoors) so students can show before they say it.
- Support: let students give the weather report with a partner, each saying one part, and use the three frames on a card.
- Stretch: ask students to add tomorrow's forecast to their report, or to tell why it is safer inside a building in a storm.
- Multilingual learners: pre-teach thunder, lightning, storm and forecast with pictures and sounds. Families can practice the report in the home language first.
- Some children are frightened of storms. Keep the tone calm and practical: storms are a normal part of weather, and grown-ups have a plan to keep everyone safe. Follow your school's drill procedures exactly.

FAMILY NOTE (send home at the start of the unit)
This week we are learning to stay safe in any weather. Our class rule is "when thunder roars, go indoors." Talk with your child about your family's plan: where would you go if a storm came? Check a weather forecast together and decide what to wear tomorrow. Ask your child to give you a weather report at breakfast!",

  "purpose": "context",
  "title": "Teacher guide: Stay Safe in Any Weather",
